citation: (1) GitLab Docs, 'AI audit events', https://docs.gitlab.com/user/ai-governance/ai-audit-events/ and 'AI governance', https://docs.gitlab.com/user/ai-governance/ (accessed 2026-10-16). (2) TierZero, 'AI agent audit trail' blog, https://www.tierzero.ai/blog/ai-agent-audit-trail/ (article dated 2026-04-13), citing an unnamed '2026 survey of over 900 security leaders' labelled 'CSA/RSAC 2026'. (3) OWASP GenAI, 'OWASP Top 10 for Agentic Applications for 2026', https://genai.owasp.org/resource/owasp-top-10-for-agentic-applications-for-2026/ (listing dated 2025-12-09).
source_tier: Vendor product documentation (GitLab); vendor blog citing a secondary survey (TierZero); practitioner standards body listing page (OWASP). No peer-reviewed source.
access_status: GitLab pages fetched via summarising fetch, not read verbatim in full. TierZero page fetched, survey itself NOT opened. OWASP landing page fetched; it contained no logging text and the full PDF was not opened. Other statistics (21% runtime visibility, 33% no audit trail, 17% reconstruct tool calls) are search snippet only. [uncertain]
sponsor_and_incentive: GitLab sells the governance features it documents. TierZero is an agent-ops vendor selling audit tooling. Survey sponsor not stated on the page. OWASP is a nonprofit community project.
exact_quotes: GitLab AI governance page: "Browse and filter a unified record of agent activity for compliance and governance purposes." GitLab AI audit events page (as returned by summarising fetch, partly paraphrased): "Each agent session produces a comprehensive audit artifact that you can inspect."; "AI audit event storage is disabled by default"; for flows such as business logic scanning, "no prompts, responses, or tool content"; feature is in beta and "subject to change without notice." TierZero: "68% of organizations cannot distinguish AI agent actions from human actions after the fact." (page body; secondary). OWASP: no logging quote obtained.
date_and_recency: GitLab docs live as of 2026-10-16 (no publication date). TierZero article 2026-04-13; underlying survey dated only '2026'. OWASP list published 2025-12-09 (within 12 months).
key_claims: 1) GitLab offers an AI audit events feature giving a chronological audit artifact per agent session, attributing composite-identity sessions to a service account with human_author_* fields recording the human who started it. 2) Storage is off by default, it is beta, and some flows record only status, timing, model and tool names with no prompts, responses or tool content. 3) Vendor-cited survey: most organisations cannot tell after the fact whether a human or an agent took an action. 4) Secondary sources say OWASP agentic guidance treats traceability as a control; specific item IDs conflicted across sources and were not verified.
headline_figures: TierZero: 68% cannot distinguish agent from human actions after the fact (survey of 'over 900 security leaders and practitioners', 2026, unnamed; secondary). Search snippets only, unverified: 21% had runtime visibility and 33% no audit trail (VentureBeat via Waxell); 17% could reconstruct full tool-call sequence (Prefactor blog, Q1 2026, 420 orgs, origin unconfirmed). Note TierZero search snippet said 'two in three' while page says 68%; consistent. [uncertain]
sample_unit_and_population: Survey figures: organisations or security practitioners, about 900 respondents for the 68% figure, enterprise security audience; methodology not seen. [uncertain] GitLab docs: no sample, product description.
observed_vs_stated: Stated: survey self-reports and vendor documentation of capabilities. No observed behaviour of what is actually logged in practice was found. The GitLab 'traceability finding' mentioned in the brief was NOT located.
what_makes_trust_justified: Per GitLab docs: per-session audit artifacts, agent identity separate from the human who started it (service account plus human_author fields), and tool allow/ask/deny policy enforced at execution. Per secondary OWASP commentary: logs naming initiating user, agent identity, target resource, action and outcome, with tool chains linked to original intent and tamper-evident storage. [uncertain]
what_it_costs: GitLab: storage must be explicitly enabled, Owner role needed to view, Premium/Ultimate tier, self-managed needs gateway config. Reviewer time to read logs is not quantified in any source found.
failure_mode_class: Security and accountability gap: inability to attribute or reconstruct actions after the fact.
control_that_would_have_prevented: Not an incident source. Reuse note: the openai-huggingface-agent-incident folder verified that OpenAI's account of its own agents' behaviour rests partly on pages that returned 403 and press paraphrase, and its research reports models tampering with logs against a grader; this supports tamper-evident logs held outside the agent's control, but only as an inference, not a verified finding. [uncertain]
limitations_stated: GitLab: beta, 'subject to change without notice', `glab govern audit` described as experimental and not ready for production (search summary of man page). Metadata-only flows omit content.
counter_evidence: Logging exists but is off by default and content-free in some flows, so a feature being available is not evidence it is used. Vendor survey figures are inconsistent in origin and could not be traced to a primary publication.
verification_status: GitLab audit-events claims: checked against the GitLab page opened (summarised, not verbatim). 68% figure: checked only that TierZero says it; survey not opened [uncertain]. 21%/33%/17% figures: not checked [uncertain]. OWASP logging requirements and item ID: not checked [uncertain]. GitLab 'traceability finding': not found [uncertain].
usable_claim: GitLab documents an agent audit-events feature that is in beta and disabled by default, and in some flows records tool names and timing but not tool content. A vendor blog cites a 2026 survey saying 68% of organisations cannot tell after the fact whether an agent or a human acted.
do_not_use: The 21%, 33% and 17% figures; any OWASP item number or quoted logging requirement; any claim of a GitLab traceability finding; any claim of what teams log in practice.
overlap_with_existing_essays: Not checked against the Verification Gap or Checking Isn't Catching essays. [uncertain]
